numerical_failure.observed_behavior: Rolling correlation/cov can produce incorrect numerical results (rolling correlation can become inf instead of matching the non-rolling result; rolling covariance/correlation are not equal to the corresponding Series.corr/cov). The Cython implementation includes an explicit NaN behavior for cases where nobs < minp or where nobs/ssqdm indicate undefined correlation/cov.
numerical_failure.expected_behavior: Rolling correlation and rolling covariance should match the vanilla correlation/covariance: for the provided example, the assertions should pass (c1 == c2 and v1 == v2). For rolling correlation, when the standard deviation components are zero/undefined, the implementation returns NaN ("Returning a nan as what the vanilla corr does is fine").
trigger_conditions: Rolling correlation/covariance on a constant sequence for one input (example: a = pd.Series([1e5, 0, 0, 0, 0])) together with a non-constant other sequence (b = pd.Series([9.45] * 5))
When the standard deviation of a constant sequence is 0, leading to a 0/0 situation for correlation (the issue notes this would produce inf in the rolling corr case, while vanilla returns nan).

Rolling window bounds where numerical instability is possible; the fix mentions "numerically_unstable" and an incremental algorithm for co-moments for numerical stability, implying the discrepancy appears under numerically unstable incremental computation conditions.

input_output_examples.input: a = pd.Series([1e5, 0, 0, 0, 0]); b = pd.Series([9.45] * 5); c1 = a.rolling(5).corr(b).iloc[4]; c2 = a.corr(b); v1 = a.rolling(5).cov(b).iloc[4]; v2 = a.cov(b)
input_output_examples.buggy_output: rolling correlation c1 can be inf while c2 is fine ("This causes inf in rolling correlation (c1 vs. c2, where c2 is fine but c1 is "wrong")"). Also v1 != v2 ("I'd assume v1 == v2 is true but it turns out not").
input_output_examples.expected_output: assert c1 == c2 and assert v1 == v2 should pass; additionally, returning NaN is acceptable for the undefined correlation case ("Returning a nan as what the vanilla corr does is fine, but returning inf is annoying and misleading").

oracle_clues: Issue #24019 expects rolling corr/cov to equal Series.corr/cov for the provided input via assertions.
The passage states the standard deviation of a constant sequence is 0, correlation would be a 0/0, and vanilla corr returns NaN; the rolling corr produced inf and is considered wrong.
The Cython code for calc_corr returns NaN when nobs <= 0.0 or ssqdm_x == 0.0 or ssqdm_y == 0.0.
The rolling covariance/correlation computation uses an incremental algorithm with numerically_unstable handling to address "numerical stability".

numerical_characteristics.magnitude: degenerate regime where stddev component is 0 due to constant sequence: a = [1e5, 0, 0, 0, 0] and b = [9.45]*5 with rolling window=5
category_specific_evidence: GH#24019 repro: a = pd.Series([1e5, 0, 0, 0, 0]); b = pd.Series([9.45] * 5); c1 = a.rolling(5).corr(b).iloc[4]; c2 = a.corr(b); v1 = a.rolling(5).cov(b).iloc[4]; v2 = a.cov(b); expected: assert c1 == c2 and assert v1 == v2.

Problem description: rolling correlation becomes inf (c1 is “wrong”) while vanilla corr (c2) is fine; constant sequence has stddev 0 so correlation is 0/0; returning NaN is fine but returning inf is misleading.

Regression test added: test_rolling_cov_corr_degenerate parametrizes method in ["corr","cov"] with expected_values: for "corr" => [np.nan]*5; for "cov" => [np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, 0.0]; inputs a = Series([1e5,0,0,0,0]) and b = Series([9.45]*5); wind = a.rolling(5). result is compared exactly via tm.assert_series_equal.
Cython aggregation implementation: output is allocated as np.empty(N, dtype=np.float64).
Cython calc_corr behavior: if nobs <= 0.0 or ssqdm_x == 0.0 or ssqdm_y == 0.0, calc_corr returns NaN (so in the degenerate constant-sequence/0-denominator regime it should be NaN rather than inf).
Cython rolling computation uses an incremental algorithm with numerically_unstable handling for numerical stability (variables numerically_unstable and requires_recompute appear in the update logic).
reproduction_risks: Evidence specifies exact inputs (a=[1e5,0,0,0,0], b=[9.45]*5) and exact rolling window size 5; reproductions using different window sizes or different magnitudes may not hit the same degenerate 0/0 regime behavior.
The discrepancy tolerance is not described; the regression test compares exact equality to expected NaN/0.0 values using tm.assert_series_equal, so using approximate comparisons may hide issues.
Evidence only states the internal output dtype is float64; reproductions that change dtype away from float64 may not follow the same path/behavior.
